extracted.intended_audience: journalists, health communicators, public health researchers and policy-makers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative metrics for newspaper reporting of theoretical (uncertain) health risks, derived from a content analysis of Canadian daily newspapers covering potential blood transmission of CJD. Focuses on what to report, how to report evidence, and how coverage can influence policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: State that the risk is theoretical
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the media reports theoretical risks, clear statements should be made that the risk is actually theoretical and not formally documented."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make an explicit, clear statement in the article that a risk is theoretical (not proven). Use unambiguous language so readers understand uncertainty; avoid implying documented causation when evidence is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine published evidence with expert opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reporting of these risks should combine published evidence with expert opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on experts' statements or solely on research—present both perspectives. Where published studies exist, summarize their findings alongside expert commentary to provide context and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite sources of published evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "When published evidence is provided, the source of the evidence should be presented where possible to give the reader the option to review the original study."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide references, journal names, study authors, dates or links when mentioning scientific studies so readers (and other stakeholders) can verify and assess the original evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: "Journals can improve the uptake of research by the lay press by press-releasing articles, although the media should not rely solely on press releases due to their selective reporting of study findings [38]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat press releases as one source among many; verify claims, seek the original paper, and corroborate with independent experts or other studies to avoid selective or inflated findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work collaboratively with researchers but beware of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: "We also recommend researchers work more closely with journalists to assist them in identifying and appraising relevant scientific information on risk."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage accessible contact between journalists and researchers to improve accuracy and timeliness. At the same time, recognize that researchers may have agendas—cross-check and seek independent commentary when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide formal training for journalists in interpreting medical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Providing journalists with formal training on how to interpret medical evidence on causation would also assist them in reporting stories on theoretical health risks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should provide or facilitate training in study design, levels of evidence, causation vs association, and how to read epidemiological studies so reporters can evaluate and contextualize research findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about absolute vs relative risk
rubrics_metrics.description: "The choice of the media to report relative as opposed to absolute risks associated with a potential harmful agent can magnify the public's perception of the risk associated with exposure to the agent [9]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting quantitative risk, present absolute risks (and denominators) or explicitly state whether figures are relative; explain the practical meaning to avoid inadvertent magnification of perceived danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance raising awareness with avoiding unnecessary alarm
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must "balance their responsibility to raise awareness of potential health threats with not unnecessarily arousing fear amongst the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories so they inform without sensationalizing. Use clear qualifiers about uncertainty, avoid alarmist language where evidence is weak, and present actionable context (e.g., incidence, transmission likelihood) when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensational headlines and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples showed headlines such as "Blood Inquiry gets new warning on killer virus that attacks brain" which can amplify fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines and leads should avoid hyperbolic phrasing that overstates unknown or theoretical risks. Ensure headline accurately reflects evidence and caveats presented in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and report type of evidence used
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting of evidence should be classified under: "general statement of risk, expert opinion, animal evidence, case report, and epidemiological study."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing evidence, explicitly state its type and level (e.g., single case report vs large epidemiological study vs animal model). This helps readers gauge the strength of the evidence and prevents conflation of weak and strong findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reporting of epidemiological (higher-level) evidence when available
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes only 11% (28 of 245) of articles referred to scientific study evidence; only 5 referenced epidemiological studies, which indicated lack of evidence for transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give priority and appropriate prominence to well-designed epidemiological studies and systematic reviews when they exist; indicate when such studies show no association so public perception aligns with best evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record article characteristics and prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Content-analysis headings used: "newspaper, date, location of article, author of article, individuals cited, organizations cited, event reported, reporting of evidence, and slant of reporting." Article placement (banner headline, front page, section) and article type (news report, information piece, human-interest, editorial) were recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reporting by documenting metadata (who wrote it, where it ran, prominence, and article type) because placement and prominence affect public recall and policy influence (availability heuristic). Use these metrics when assessing media impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record slant and critique of decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles were coded for "slant of reporting" including whether they were "critical of decision-making" or "supported decision-making", and identified sources of criticism/praise (paper/author, advocacy group, individual/victim, expert, unidentified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage presents critique or support for policy decisions and identify the voices driving the slant. This helps analyze media influence on policy and the balance of perspectives portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about limitations journalists face
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often "lack expertise in appraising evidence and [face] time pressures" which makes expert opinion more accessible and understandable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing reporting, be transparent about journalists' constraints (time, resources, expertise). Newsrooms should disclose when specialists were consulted or when definitive evidence was unavailable, and news organizations should consider editorial practices that allow proper vetting of complex medical stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate formats (qualitative vs quantitative) mindful of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: "Qualitative descriptions of risk ... have also been demonstrated to be better understood by the public than quantitative descriptions [34]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, combine qualitative explanations (which the public may find easier to grasp) with clear quantitative context (absolute risk figures) so stories are both understandable and accurate.
